intro.caption: Lesson 4-5 — determine the whole given the part and percent. Thirty pairs of sneakers vanished overnight, and the shipping slip only says that 30 pairs was 25% of the drop. How big was the whole drop?

balloons.t: Thirty pairs are gone! And the slip says that was 25 percent of our drop!
Somebody check the door. Also, check Sly's alibi.
30 pairs is only the 25% PART. The 100% whole drop must be bigger than 30.
Put 25% and 30 in a ratio table, then scale both columns up to 100%!
When 60% is $48, find 10% first by dividing by 6. Then multiply by 10!
Or divide the part by the decimal percent: 48 ÷ 0.60. Same answer!
If 16 pairs is 20%, the whole drop is 16 × 0.2 = 3.2 pairs!
3.2 pairs is SMALLER than 16! You multiplied when you needed to divide.
I only have 18 pairs left, and that's 50% of what I brought — so I started with 9!
Hold it, Sly. Check his numbers and crack the last two clues!
120 pairs in the drop, every sneaker accounted for, and my calculator is undefeated.

win.caption: When you know the part and its percent, work backwards to the 100% whole using an equivalent ratio table or whole = part ÷ percent — never multiply the part by the percent.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Build the Table
gates.prompt: 30 pairs vanished, and that was 25% of the drop. Reason about size first, then scale to 100%.
hints: Conceptual: when the percent is less than 100%, the given number is only a part, so the 100% whole must be larger.
Procedural: pair 25% with 30 in a ratio table, then multiply both numbers by 4 to reach 100%.

steps: Practice clue: 12 caps is 20% of a crate.
The whole crate holds 60 caps. Check: 0.20 × 60 = 12.
worked.q: If 14 hoodies are 50% of a rack, how many hoodies are on the whole rack?

items.q: 30 pairs vanished, and that was 25% of the drop. Before computing, is the whole drop more or less than 30 pairs?

options.t: Less than 30 pairs, because 25% means divide 30 by 4
options.fb: 30 is the 25% part, not the whole drop! The 100% whole must be bigger than 30.

options.t: Equal to 30 pairs, because 30 is the total
options.fb: 30 is only the 25% that vanished, not 100% of the drop.

options.t: More than 30 pairs, because 30 is only 25% of the 100% drop
Zero pairs, because they sold out
options.fb: We want the size of the original 100% drop before the 30 pairs vanished.

items.label: 25% is 30 pairs. Scale to 100%: whole drop = (pairs)
items.aria: total pairs in the whole drop when thirty pairs is twenty five percent

fb.msg: 7.5 is 30 × 0.25! That multiplied the part by the percent, making the whole smaller than 30.
55 adds 30 + 25. Scale 25% up to 100% by multiplying both by 4.

gates.pass: 120 pairs in the drop! Now we know how big the shipment really was.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Find the Whole
gates.prompt: Use 10%-steps or divide the part by the decimal percent to recover the original whole.
hints: Conceptual: if you know 60% of a price, 10% is one sixth of that part, and ten 10%-steps make 100%.
Procedural: divide the part by the first digit to get 10% then multiply by 10 — or compute part ÷ decimal.

steps: Practice price: $42 is 60% of the original price.
worked.q: 18 pairs is 30% of how many pairs?

items.label: A jacket on sale costs $48, which is 60% of the original price. Original price = ($)
items.aria: original price when forty eight dollars is sixty percent

fb.msg: 28.8 is 48 × 0.6 — you multiplied the part by the percent! Divide 48 by 0.6.
$8 is 10% of the original price. Multiply $8 by 10 to reach 100%.
108 adds 48 + 60. Divide 48 by 6 to get 10%, then multiply by 10.

items.fbDefault: Find 10% first (48 ÷ 6 = 8), then multiply by 10 (or compute 48 ÷ 0.6).

items.label: 36 hats sold, which is 40% of the hat shipment. Whole shipment = (hats)
items.aria: total hats in shipment when thirty six hats is forty percent

fb.msg: 14.4 is 36 × 0.4. Here 36 is the part, so divide 36 by 0.4.
9 is 10% of the shipment. Multiply by 10 to reach 100%.

gates.pass: $80 jacket and 90 hats! Every clue is lining up.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Judge & Check
gates.prompt: Judge Ruben's claim, then check Hye-jin's answer by multiplying back to the part.
hints: Conceptual: multiplying the part by the percent makes an answer smaller than the part, which fails the size check.
Procedural: to check any whole, multiply decimal percent × whole and see if it lands on the given part.

steps: Practice check: is 21 equal to 70% of 30?
It lands on 21, so 30 is verified as the whole.
worked.q: Check: if 35 is 50% of 70, what is 0.50 × 70?

items.q: Ruben says 16 pairs is 20% of 3.2 pairs ("16 × 0.2 = 3.2!"). Tasha says 80 pairs. Who is right?

options.fb: 3.2 is smaller than the 16-pair part! Multiplying by 0.20 finds 20% OF 16, not the whole.

options.t: Tasha: 0.20 × 80 = 16, and the whole must be bigger than 16

options.fb: Adding 16 + 20 ignores the percent ratio. Check with 0.20 × whole = 16.

items.label: Check Hye-jin's claim that 45 pairs is 75% of 60 pairs. Compute 0.75 × 60 =
items.aria: check seventy five percent of sixty pairs

fb.msg: 80 is 60 ÷ 0.75. Here you are checking by multiplying 0.75 × 60.

gates.pass: Tasha is right (80 pairs), and 0.75 × 60 = 45! Time to corner Sly.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Size the Drop
gates.prompt: Solve the last two inventory clues and judge Sly's suitcase claim.
hints: Conceptual: when you have the part and its percent, divide the part by the decimal percent to get the 100% whole.
Procedural: scale to 100% using 10%-steps or compute part ÷ decimal, then check by multiplying.

steps: Practice clue: 24 boxes is 30% of a truckload.
worked.q: 15 pairs is 25% of how many pairs?

items.label: Clue 1 · 14 pairs is 20% of a shelf. Whole shelf = (pairs)
items.aria: total pairs on shelf when fourteen pairs is twenty percent

fb.msg: 2.8 is 14 × 0.20 — don't multiply the part by the percent! Divide 14 by 0.20.
7 is 10% of the shelf. Multiply by 10 to reach 100%.

items.label: Clue 2 · 63 hoodies sold, which is 70% of the drop. Whole drop = (hoodies)
items.aria: total hoodies in drop when sixty three hoodies is seventy percent

fb.msg: 44.1 is 63 × 0.70. Divide 63 by 0.70 to find the whole.
9 is 10% of the drop. Multiply by 10 to reach 100%.

items.q: Final Verdict · Sly has 18 pairs left, which is 50% of his suitcase, and claims he started with 9 pairs. Judge his claim!

options.fb: 9 is 50% OF 18. If 18 is 50% of his suitcase, the whole suitcase held twice as many: 36!
Adding 18 + 50 ignores the 50% ratio. 50% is half, so double 18.
50% of the whole is 18, so the whole is 18 ÷ 0.50 = 36, not 18 ÷ 2.

options.t: False! 18 is 50%, so he started with 36 pairs (18 ÷ 0.50)

gates.pass: BOOM! 70 pairs, 90 hoodies, and Sly's 36-pair suitcase exposed! Case closed.

journal.heading: Lesson 4-5 — what the sold-out mystery taught us
rows: When the percent is under 100%, the given number is only a part, so the 100% whole must be LARGER.
Use a ratio table or 10%-steps: if 60% is $48, then 10% is $8, and 100% is $80.
Since percent × whole = part, find the whole by dividing: whole = part ÷ percent.
Multiplying 30 × 0.25 gives 7.5 (smaller than 30!). Never multiply the part by the percent when the whole is missing.
journal.quote: "If your whole comes out smaller than your part, you multiplied when you should have divided." — Hye-jin

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 4-5 (Determine the Whole Given the Part and Percent) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. Covers ratio tables, 10%-steps, dividing by the decimal percent, and checking by multiplying.
standards: Use equivalent ratio tables and equations to determine the whole given a part and percent
